record.paper_title: On an unsolved problem from the theory of Boolean algebras
record.original_question: Let A be a set and let S(A) denote the Boolean algebra of all subsets of A. A principal ideal of S(A) is the ideal consisting of all subsets of one fixed subset X of A. Suppose A has cardinality less than the first aleph inaccessible in the weak sense, with the parallel strict-sense variant stated in the source. Is every sigma-ideal I of S(A) for which the quotient Boolean algebra S(A)/I is complete necessarily principal?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a nonempty set and let $S(A)$ denote the Boolean algebra $(\mathcal{P}(A), \cup, \cap, \setminus, \emptyset, A)$ of all subsets of $A$. An ideal $I \subseteq S(A)$ is called a $\sigma$-ideal if it is closed under countable unions, i.e. whenever $\{X_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \subseteq I$ one has $\bigcup_n X_n \in I$. An ideal $I$ is called principal if there exists a fixed subset $X_0 \subseteq A$ such that $I = \{Y \subseteq A : Y \subseteq X_0\}$. The quotient Boolean algebra $S(A)/I$ is called complete if every subset of $S(A)/I$ has a supremum in $S(A)/I$.

Recall that an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ is weakly inaccessible if it is a regular limit cardinal, and strongly inaccessible if in addition $2^\lambda < \kappa$ for every $\lambda < \kappa$. Let $\aleph^w$ denote the least weakly inaccessible cardinal and $\aleph^s$ the least strongly inaccessible cardinal (each treated as $\infty$ if none exists).

Question: Assume $|A| < \aleph^w$ (respectively $|A| < \aleph^s$). Is it true that every $\sigma$-ideal $I$ of $S(A)$ for which the quotient $S(A)/I$ is a complete Boolean algebra must be a principal ideal?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is classically connected to Ulam's work on measurable cardinals. The existence of a non-principal σ-ideal $I$ on a set $A$ with $S(A)/I$ complete is equivalent to the existence of a measurable cardinal $\le |A|$ (Tarski; via the theory of two-valued measurable cardinals). Since every measurable cardinal is (strongly, hence weakly) inaccessible, the assumption $|A| < \aleph^w$ (or $|A| < \aleph^s$) forces $|A|$ to be below the least measurable cardinal, and therefore every such σ-ideal is principal. Thus the question has an affirmative answer under the stated cardinality hypothesis.

status_evidence.title: Measurable cardinal — Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Ulam introduced measurable cardinals in 1930; a non-principal countably complete ultrafilter / σ-ideal on a set yields a measurable cardinal, and every measurable cardinal is inaccessible.
status_evidence.claim: Non-principal σ-ideals on $A$ with complete quotient correspond to measurable cardinals $\le |A|$, all of which are inaccessible.

status_evidence.title: Complete Boolean algebra — Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Quotients $P(A)/I$ by σ-ideals are complete Boolean algebras precisely in connection with measurable-cardinal phenomena.
status_evidence.claim: Completeness of $S(A)/I$ for nonprincipal σ-ideals requires large-cardinal strength.
